newsitem.title: USA: British nanny's mother still hopes for bail.
newsitem.headline: British nanny's mother still hopes for bail.

text.p: The mother of an 18-year-old British nanny accused of murdering a 9-month-old infant in Massachusetts told reporters on Wednesday she hoped to arrange bail for her daughter.

"She's still in shock," said Susan Woodward, who has visited her daughter, Louise, each day at Framingham prison outside Boston where she is being held on charges of killing Matthew Eappen, a baby who had been left in her care.

"Louise wants to come home. She wants to stay here, clear her name and come home and resume a normal life, a family life at home," Woodward told a news conference at her daughter's lawyer's offices. The family is from Chester, England.
Woodward said she did not understand why her daughter had been denied bail. "If she did flee, she could never do that (clear her name). Not ever. So what would be the point?" Woodward said.

A judge ordered Louise Woodward held without bail after she pleaded not guilty to a charge of first-degree murder. If convicted she faces a mandatory sentence of life in prison with no eligibility for parole.
Woodward said that her daughter was reading books, going to church and praying in prison.
"Louise finds it very difficult to cope with people dying. It's something she has not had a lot of experience of and that was one of my main concerns. How was she going to deal with death?
"But she is a committed Christian and she's been going to church while she's in prison and reading her Bible. And she's coping with it okay," Woodward said.

She said her heart went out to the parents of the victim, Sunil and Deborah Eappen. "I have no conception of what it would be like to lose a child. I have every sympathy for them and what they must be going through -- their own nightmare, as we are," she said.

Louise Woodward, who went to work for the Eappens in November, called rescue workers to her employers' home in the Boston suburb of Newton on Feb. 5 and told them the boy had suddenly stopped breathing after being sick all day. He was taken to a hospital and diagnosed with head trauma consistent with shaken-baby syndrome.
He was on life support for four days before he died of a brain haemorrhage on Feb. 9. Autopsy reports ruled the cause of death was a blunt blow to the head.
